items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: That’s called a Brownlick. That’s where I got that from.

ctx.x: Yeah. That feels good. That’s what music is supposed to feel like. That’s called a Brownlick. That’s where I got that from.

items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Clifford Brown, Dizzy Gillespie, Kenny Dorham and all these kind of guys, you know, Donald Byrd and Howard McGhee and all of these, my brother was born of that generation. So I heard great music growing up. And so when I play, I try to emulate the best sounds that I’ve heard.

ctx.x: Yes, well thank you. It’s — my dad was a trumpet player, a really great trumpet player. He went to Juilliard Conservatory and he played in the, like I said earlier, he played with Cab Calloway, the Billy Eckstine band, the Walter Fats Pichon band, which is a band few people have heard of but that was a killer band. They played on the S.S. Dixie. They went up and down the Mississippi River. Man, Fats Pichon was a great writer, and he taught my dad a lot after my dad got out of Juilliard. I mean you know you learn…

Holiday and all of that stuff. So I grew up listening to really good music. I mean quite naturally, in the late ‘60s and early 70s when I started, I was a little teenager and I started first playing, and I played in all these rock bands you know. We were trying to play like Chicago and Blood Sweat and Tears type of stuff, which I thought was very well constructed music, still. But I had heard all of these Louis Armstrong doing like “I’m in the Market for You” with all of these beautiful, high notes, just coming…

Is there anything that you can give us a word on to get more music available to young people so — jazz is considered only three percent of the record market — to get more of this great music which is of American heritage on the menu?
